title: Character eigenspaces and induction from the stabilizer for a normal subgroup with commuting image
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero [def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $G$ be a finite group, and let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}_F(V)$ be a representation on a nonzero finite-dimensional $F$-vector space with no nonzero proper $G$-invariant subspace. Let $A\trianglelefteq G$ be a normal subgroup such that $\rho(a)\rho(b)=\rho(b)\rho(a)$ for all $a,b\in A$; $A$ itself need not be abelian. For a homomorphism $\chi:A\to F^\times$ put
$$V_\chi=\{v\in V:\rho(a)v=\chi(a)v\text{ for every }a\in A\},\qquad X=\{\chi:V_\chi\ne0\}.$$
The set $X$ is finite and nonempty, and $V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in X}V_\chi$ as $F$-vector spaces. The rule $(g\chi)(a)=\chi(g^{-1}ag)$ defines a transitive action of $G$ on $X$, with $\rho(g)V_\chi=V_{g\chi}$. For each $\chi\in X$ let $T_\chi=\{g\in G:g\chi=\chi\}$. Then $A\leq T_\chi$, the restricted action on $V_\chi$ is an irreducible $T_\chi$-representation, and the canonical map
$$\operatorname{Ind}_{T_\chi}^G V_\chi\longrightarrow V,\qquad [g]\otimes v\longmapsto\rho(g)v$$
is an isomorphism of $G$-representations. Here induction is the quotient of $F[G]\otimes_F V_\chi$ by the relations $[gt]\otimes v=[g]\otimes\rho(t)v$, with left translation on $[g]$, and $F[G]$ has basis $[g]$ indexed by $G$.

source.place: Lemma 16.11, printed p.327, common-eigenvector argument; forming the character from its eigenvalues is the explicit agent calculation here.

proof.text: Normality ensures $g^{-1}ag\in A$, so $g\chi$ is a character. For $g,h\in G$ and $a\in A$, $((gh)\chi)(a)=\chi(h^{-1}g^{-1}agh)=(g(h\chi))(a)$, and $1\chi=\chi$. If $w\in V_\chi$, then $\rho(a)\rho(g)w=\rho(g)\rho(g^{-1}ag)w=\chi(g^{-1}ag)\rho(g)w$. Hence $\rho(g)V_\chi\subseteq V_{g\chi}$; applying the same calculation to $g^{-1}$ gives equality. Invertibility preserves nonzero subspaces, so this action restricts to $X$.

proof.text: For $a,b\in A$ and $c\in F$, commutativity gives $(\rho(b)-c\,\mathrm{id})^n\rho(a)=\rho(a)(\rho(b)-c\,\mathrm{id})^n$ by induction on $n$. Thus $\rho(a)$ preserves every maximal generalized eigenspace of $\rho(b)$. Apply [lem-per-compatible-generalized-weight-independence] with $K=F$, $M=V$, $I=A$ and $f_a=\rho(a)$. For any character $\chi$, its ordinary eigenspace $V_\chi$ is contained in $W_{\lambda_\chi}$, where $\lambda_\chi(a)$ is the scalar underlying $\chi(a)$ (take exponent $1$ in each generalized-eigenspace equation). Distinct characters give distinct functions $\lambda_\chi$. Therefore a finite relation among vectors from distinct $V_\chi$ is a relation in distinct independent $W_{\lambda_\chi}$ and all its components vanish. This proves independence of the character eigenspaces.

proof.text: Let $O=G\chi_0$, a finite nonempty orbit because $G$ is finite, and put $S=\sum_{\eta\in O}V_\eta$. Step 2 shows $\rho(g)S=S$ for every $g\in G$, and Step 1 gives $S\ne0$. Irreducibility forces $S=V$. If $\psi\in X\setminus O$ and $0\ne w\in V_\psi$, write $w=\sum_{\eta\in O}w_\eta$ using $S=V$. Independence from Step 3 applied to $w-\sum w_\eta=0$ gives $w=0$, a contradiction. Hence $X=O$, so $X$ is finite and the action is transitive. The spanning equality and independence say precisely $V=\bigoplus_{\eta\in X}V_\eta$.

proof.text: Fix $\chi\in X$ and write $T=T_\chi$. The action law makes $T$ a subgroup: $1\chi=\chi$, and if $t\chi=\chi$ and $u\chi=\chi$, then $(tu^{-1})\chi=\chi$. For $a,b\in A$, the homomorphism law gives $\chi(a^{-1}ba)=\chi(a)^{-1}\chi(b)\chi(a)=\chi(b)$ in the abelian group $F^\times$. Thus $A\leq T$, without requiring $A$ abelian. By Step 2, $\rho(t)V_\chi=V_\chi$ for $t\in T$, so restriction defines the asserted $T$-representation.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation-lifting context only. Agent-written auxiliary representation argument; the missing Serre source is recorded in report.md.

proof.text: Choose representatives $R$ for the left cosets $gT$ with the identity representing $T$. The map $r\mapsto r\chi$ bijects $R$ with $X$: transitivity gives surjectivity, and $r\chi=s\chi$ is equivalent to $s^{-1}r\in T$. Let $0\ne U\subseteq V_\chi$ be a $T$-invariant subspace. Then $L=\sum_{r\in R}\rho(r)U$ is $G$-invariant: writing $gr=st$ with $s\in R,t\in T$ gives $\rho(g)\rho(r)U=\rho(s)\rho(t)U=\rho(s)U$. Thus $L=V$ by irreducibility. Each $\rho(r)U$ lies in $V_{r\chi}$. Independence, as established using [lem-per-compatible-generalized-weight-independence] in Step 3, implies $L\cap V_\chi=U$: in an expression for a vector of the intersection, all components with $r\ne1$ vanish. Since $L=V$, this yields $U=V_\chi$. The restricted representation is nonzero by $\chi\in X$ and has no nonzero proper invariant subspace.

proof.text: The rule $[g]\otimes w\mapsto\rho(g)w$ is $F$-bilinear before passing to the tensor product, and $\rho(gt)w=\rho(g)\rho(t)w$ shows that it annihilates every defining induction relation. It therefore defines a linear map $\Phi:\operatorname{Ind}_T^G V_\chi\to V$. It is $G$-equivariant because $\Phi([hg]\otimes w)=\rho(h)\rho(g)w$. Its image contains $\rho(r)V_\chi=V_{r\chi}$ for every $r\in R$ and hence spans $V$ by Step 4. Thus $\Phi$ is surjective.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation-lifting context only. Agent-written auxiliary representation argument; the missing Serre source is recorded in report.md.

proof.text: For $x\in V$, use the unique decomposition $x=\sum_{r\in R}x_r$ with $x_r\in V_{r\chi}$ from Step 4, whose uniqueness follows from [lem-per-compatible-generalized-weight-independence] as in Step 3. Define $\Psi(x)=\sum_{r\in R}[r]\otimes\rho(r^{-1})x_r$ in the induction quotient; Step 2 puts every coefficient in $V_\chi$. Uniqueness of the components shows that they depend linearly on $x$, so $\Psi$ is linear and $\Phi\Psi(x)=\sum_r x_r=x$. For a generating tensor $[g]\otimes w$, write $g=rt$ with $r\in R,t\in T$. The only component of $\rho(g)w$ is in $V_{r\chi}$, so $\Psi\Phi([g]\otimes w)=[r]\otimes\rho(t)w=[rt]\otimes w=[g]\otimes w$ by the defining relation. These tensors span the quotient, hence $\Psi\Phi=\mathrm{id}$. This proves that the specified canonical $G$-equivariant map is an isomorphism.
